implementation_notes: The JDK ships the forwarding mechanism: Proxy.newProxyInstance(classLoader, new Class<?>[]{Dir.class}, handler) returns a proxy instance that implements exactly the interfaces named at creation, and every call on it - including hashCode, equals and toString - is dispatched to InvocationHandler.invoke, which is where the membrane wraps arguments, forwards to the target and wraps results. Proxy instances cover interfaces only, so a membrane over a final class needs bytecode generation (ByteBuddy/ASM) or a hand-written forwarding class. Identity and revocation stay yours: keep the per-membrane identity map weakly keyed on the wrapped object so one target yields one proxy and the map does not pin it, and check a volatile or AtomicBoolean revocation flag inside invoke, in the same synchronized or atomic step as the forward so a revoked membrane cannot serve an in-flight call.
pitfalls: A proxy implements only the interfaces listed at creation: methods of the concrete class that are not on the interface stay reachable to anyone holding the raw reference, and the two-argument equals/hashCode/toString calls are dispatched to your handler, so a naive handler breaks collection semantics.
Method.invoke wraps exceptions thrown by the target in InvocationTargetException; unwrap them or callers see a different exception type than the interface declares.

The identity map must be weakly keyed and must not strongly reference proxies, or the registry pins the wrapped graph and revocation leaks it; reflection also costs a varargs array and a dispatch per call, so keep the mediated path lean.
